blogs.title: Who Gets the Penalty? The Eighth Circuit Reads Minnesota’s Payment of Wages Act as a Commissioner-Only Remedy
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s holding that the ‘average daily wage’ penalty in Minn. Stat. § 181.101 is not privately recoverable by employees, even though employees may sue for unpaid wages under § 181.171. It would focus on the opinion’s textualist move—contrasting § 181.101 with §§ 181.13 and 181.14, where the legislature expressly authorizes employees to ‘charge and collect’ penalties—and consider what this means for private wage litigation in Minnesota going forward.

blogs.title: Laidlaw in the Wage-and-Hour Context: Standing and Mootness After the Employer Pays Everything Owed
blogs.description: This post would examine the most consequential federal-courts issue in the case: whether an employee who has already received all overtime wages and liquidated damages can still pursue statutory penalties payable to the state. It would unpack the panel’s remand under Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw, the importance of whether Consilio’s overtime policy remains in place, and Judge Kobes’s separate suggestion that the real problem may be standing rather than mootness.

blogs.title: When ‘Wage Theft’ Is Not a Penalty Claim: The Narrow Private Reach of Minnesota’s Notice Provisions
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s treatment of the Minnesota Wage Theft Act claim, highlighting the gap between statutory notice obligations and privately recoverable remedies. It would explain why the court was unwilling to infer penalties from the notice provisions once Cohen had been paid, and how the opinion may limit attempts to convert technical payroll-notice violations into high-value penalty suits absent clear legislative authorization.

blogs.title: You Can’t Amend a Wage Case in a Summary Judgment Brief
blogs.description: This post would use the rejected request for injunctive relief to explore a quieter but important procedural lesson of the case: remedial theories must be pleaded, preserved, and litigated consistently. It would discuss the parties’ stipulations, the consequences of narrowing a case to penalties after accepting full individual payment, and the Eighth Circuit’s reminder that new forms of relief belong in an amended complaint—not in opposition briefing.
